paras: The lynching of Juan Elverad took place in Socorro, New Mexico Territory, in mid-August 1882, when a crowd took a man accused of raping an eight-year-old girl from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. A coroner's inquest found that he died 'at the hands of unknown parties,' and wire reports carried the hanging across the country under approving headlines.

The accused, described as a gambler and in one brief as a 'monte gambler,' appears in the papers under many spellings, including Juan Elverad, Juan Alvorid, Juan Alvarid and Juan Eleverado. According to a special dispatch from Socorro to the El Paso Herald, he was arraigned before Judge Dehoum on a charge of raping Elina Weldred, the eight-year-old daughter of John Weldred, a miner. He was bound over in $5,000, which he could not give, and was placed in jail.

That night a large crowd gathered around the jail and demanded the keys from the guard, who gave them up 'after slight resistance.' The Albuquerque wire put the mob at 200 men who 'quietly took him from jail,' while an Arizona paper said the crowd 'overpowered the jailor.' The crowd first brought the prisoner before the girl, who identified him.

The mob then marched him across the plaza to the rear of the Windsor hotel and hanged him to a tree. Asked whether he had anything to say, he reportedly answered, 'It's God's will and your wish; I die guilty, and am willing. Farewell to my friends.'

His body was cut down at eight o'clock the next morning, and an inquest returned a verdict of 'Death from hanging at the hands of unknown parties.' The Albuquerque wire reported 'very little excitement over the occurrence,' and no report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or prosecution of the mob appears in the coverage.

Two separate dispatches carried the story: a brief Albuquerque wire dated August 18, printed in papers from Washington to Sacramento, and a fuller El Paso Herald special from Socorro dated August 17, run by Texas papers. Headline writers treated the hanging as deserved: the Yankton Press and Dakotaian titled the wire 'SERVED HIM RIGHT.' and the Sacramento Record-Union called it 'A Dastardly Outrage Promptly Punished.' The Memphis Public Ledger ran it under 'Judge Lynch,' and a Baltimore German-language daily translated the same wire.

Within a week the story had shrunk to one-line items in weekly crime digests, which spelled the name Juan Everard or Juan Elverad. Early in September the Arizona Weekly Citizen wrote that 'The citizens of Socorro' had lynched him and joked that he had 'gone to join the Guiteau band in glory.' None of the coverage gives the race of the hanged man or of the crowd.

The dates differ: the Socorro special has him arraigned on the evening of August 16 and hanged that night, while the Albuquerque wire dates his arrest to August 17 and the hanging to the following night. Other briefs place the hanging on Thursday night, August 17, and one Arizona paper puts both the alleged assault and the hanging on that Thursday. One Iowa weekly gave the girl's age as 12 rather than eight, and two Arizona papers named the tree as a peach tree and a pear tree.

accounts.label: Albuquerque wire
accounts.gist: A gambler outraged an eight-year-old girl Sunday night, was arrested 'yesterday morning' and jailed under $5,000 bonds; that night a mob of 200 quietly took him to the girl, who identified him, and hanged him to a tree amid 'very little excitement'.

accounts.label: El Paso Herald special from Socorro
accounts.gist: Arraigned 'yesterday evening' before Judge Dehoum and jailed for want of $5,000 bail, Alvorid was taken that night by an immense crowd that got the keys from the guard, identified by the girl, and hanged behind the Windsor hotel after saying 'I die guilty'; an inquest blamed unknown parties.

accounts.label: Arizona Miner brief
accounts.gist: Elvered outraged the girl 'last Thursday' and that evening 200 men overpowered the jailor and hanged him to a peach tree.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'SERVED HIM RIGHT.' and 'A Dastardly Outrage Promptly Punished' presented the hanging as deserved punishment.
Texas papers ran the Socorro special in full, including the man's reported admission 'I die guilty' and the inquest verdict, without comment.
Most papers carried the Albuquerque wire or a one-line digest of it in crime columns.
The Arizona Weekly Citizen joked that the man had 'gone to join the Guiteau band in glory'.

conflicts.note: The Socorro special was dated Aug. 17 and sent from the town, so its timing is the closer source; the Albuquerque wire dated Aug. 18 may have counted 'yesterday' from its own date. Both put the hanging no earlier than Aug. 16 and no later than Aug. 18.
